Q: Private Cloud Run service returns generic HTML 404 with no request log A:

Well, looking at what you described, the key detail here is that generic HTML 404 page and the total lack of request logs.

Basically, your request is not even reaching your app container at all. It is getting stopped and rejected at Google's front door (the Google Front End / GFE load balancer) before it ever gets routed into Cloud Run.

Here is what is likely going on, mapped to your questions:

1. Why you get a generic HTML 404 with zero logs

When Google's frontend returns that classic 404 HTML page without writing anything to Cloud Run request logs, it almost always means one of these things:

  • Host header mismatch: If your HTTP client altered or stripped the original Host: header, Google’s front edge doesn't know which service you are trying to reach and just drops a generic 404.
  • Typo or missing region in the URL: If the hostname does not match an active route registered on Google's edge tables (for example, hitting an old, mistyped, or non existent hash subdomain), the frontend simply says "not found" at the infrastructure level.
  • DNS caching or propagation lag: If the service was created and tested immediately, edge routing tables occasionally take a few seconds to sync up worldwide.

Since the request never gets handed over to the Cloud Run service infrastructure, no request log or trace entry is created.

2. Are status.url and the deployment output URL both callable?

Yes, absolutely. They both point to the exact same default endpoint (https://<service>-<hash>-<region>.a.run.app). For a private service, you just need to pass a valid Authorization: Bearer <ID_TOKEN> header where the token's audience matches that base URL.

3. How to tell a frontend routing miss apart from an IAM rejection

You can easily tell them apart by the HTTP status code and response body:

  • Frontend Route Miss (404 Not Found): Returns the standard Google 404 HTML page. Zero Cloud Run logs because Google's edge doesn't recognize where to send the traffic.
  • IAM Rejection (403 Forbidden): Cloud Run's builtin auth layer will intercept the call and return a 403 Forbidden with a plain text or specific error message (e.g., Your client does not have permission to get URL...), not a generic 404.

So, um, double check your custom HTTP client to make sure it sends the full, untouched Host header matching the exact .a.run.app address, and verify there wasn't a tiny typo in the URL path or domain name.

Q: If String is a reference type, what exactly happens when we write String name = "Rahul"? A:

Your breakdown is completely spot on.

1. Is "Rahul" really an object, and does name hold a reference?

Yes, exactly that.

  • String is the blueprint (the class).
  • "Rahul" is an actual java.lang.String object created in memory.
  • name is the reference variable sitting on the stack, holding the memory address that points straight to that "Rahul" object.

2. What is actually going on under the hood?

Whenever Java hits a string literal like "Rahul", it checks a special area in the heap called the String Constant Pool:

  1. The JVM looks inside the pool to see if an identical "Rahul" object already exists.
  2. If it is already there, it reuses it. If not, it creates a new String object with the characters "Rahul" inside the pool.
  3. Finally, it assigns the memory address of that pool object to your variable name.

So name does not hold the actual characters R, a, h, u, l directly. It only holds a reference (a pointer) to where that object lives in the pool.

3. Why not write String name = new String("Rahul")?

You totally can, but Java gives us string literals as a built-in convenience and performance feature:

  • String name = "Rahul"; uses the string pool. If you create ten variables with "Rahul", all ten will point to the exact same object in memory, saving a ton of RAM.
  • String name = new String("Rahul"); forces Java to create a completely new object on the general heap every single time, completely bypassing the pool sharing and eating up unnecessary memory.

So your intuition of String (class) -> "Rahul" (object) -> name (reference variable holding the address) is 100% correct.

Q: CSS background image shows only white site A:

This is a classic relative path gotcha with CSS. When you put an inline style="..." tag in your HTML, the browser looks for the image relative to where that HTML file lives. But when you write url(...) inside a .css file, the browser looks for the image relative to the CSS file itself.

So if your stylesheet is tucked inside a folder like css/ or styles/, writing app/images/... makes the browser search inside css/app/images/... and return a 404 error.

You can fix this easily with one of these:

  1. Step out of the CSS folder using ../:
background: url("../app/images/app/bg_garden.jpg") no-repeat center center fixed;
background-size: cover;

Add more ../ if your CSS file is nested deeper in subfolders.

  1. Use an absolute path from the root directory by adding a leading slash:
background: url("/app/images/app/bg_garden.jpg") no-repeat center center fixed;
background-size: cover;

Quick tip: check the Network tab in your browser's dev tools (F12) to see the exact red 404 URL it is trying to request. Also, you can safely drop all those vendor prefixes (-webkit-, -moz-, -o-) since background-size: cover has been universally supported for years.

Q: Base + Offset Addressing Mode A:

This is what happens when performing an LDR using a base register R6 and destination register R2:

MAR<-R6 + IR[5:0]
MDR<-MEM[MAR]
R2<-MDR

Let's say R6 = x3000, IR[5:0] = x5, and R2 = 0 (although this value doesn't matter since it will be loaded with another value at the end).

MAR<-R6 + IR[5:0]

R6 is added to IR[5:0] (which is the offset value in the last six bits of the LDR instruction). The base x3000 (value of R6) has x5 (value of IR[5:0]) added to it, giving us x3005. The MAR (memory address register) now holds x3005.

MDR<-MEM[MAR]

The value in the MAR (x3005) is loaded into the MDR (memory data register).

R2<-MDR

The value in the MDR (x3005) is loaded into R2. R2 now holds the value: x3005.

Q: How to do DISTINCT on multiple columns in DAX query? A:

Just in case if this helps someone in future.

EVALUATE 
DISTINCT(
SELECTCOLUMNS('Dim_Products',
'Dim_Products'[SaleCode], 
'Dim_Products'[ProducttName],  
'Dim_TimeZone'[StartDate], 
'Dim_TimeZone'[StartTime], 
'Dim_TimeZone'[EndDate], 
'Dim_TimeZone'[EndTime], 
'Dim_TimeZone'[Variation]))

And, if we need to add a filter:

    EVALUATE 
        DISTINCT(
        SELECTCOLUMNS(
         FILTER('Dim_Products', 'Dim_Products'[SaleCode] = 123 && ('Dim_Products'[ProducttName] = "ABC" || 'Dim_Products'[ProducttName] = "XYZ" )),
        'Dim_Products'[SaleCode], 
        'Dim_Products'[ProducttName],  
        'Dim_TimeZone'[StartDate], 
        'Dim_TimeZone'[StartTime], 
        'Dim_TimeZone'[EndDate], 
        'Dim_TimeZone'[EndTime], 
        'Dim_TimeZone'[Variation]))
